# From linear regression to mixed models

<style>
  :root {
    --footer-text:  "Mixed models 1";
    --qr:           `r qr_css`;
    --lecture:      `r lecture_label`;
  }
</style>

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` naked mole-rats live underground in East Africa, in colonies of about 70 animals on average, and up to 295. Only one female, the [queen]{.hl}, breeds.

_Source: Smithsonian's National Zoo_
:::

## Today

- Repeated measures and the independence assumption
- Old solutions: averaging over participants or items
- Mixed models: varying intercepts and varying slopes
- Partial pooling: borrowing strength across groups
- Interpreting random effects, and the `lme4` syntax
- Why varying slopes matter
- What is a random effect, anyway?

## So far

Lectures 4 to 9: `lm()`, with one or several predictors, and how to test them.

. . .

Every one of those models assumed that the data points are __independent__: each one brings new information.

. . .

In linguistics, that is almost never true.

## Repeated measures

Data have [repeated measures]{.hl} when the same units, such as participants, speakers, words or schools, are measured more than once. A participant responds to many words, each word is read by many participants, and a speaker produces many tokens of the same vowel.

. . .

Measurements from the same unit tend to be more alike than measurements from different units. That breaks the independence assumption of linear regression.

## The data {.smaller}

A simulated lexical decision experiment: 20 participants each respond to the same 40 words.

```{r}
set.seed(21)
n_subj <- 20
n_item <- 40

z0 <- rnorm(n_subj)
z1 <- rnorm(n_subj)
participants <- tibble(participant = sprintf("P%02d", 1:n_subj),
                       u0 = 70 * z0,                                   # own speed
                       u1 = 18 * (-0.6 * z0 + sqrt(1 - 0.36) * z1))    # own frequency effect
words <- tibble(word     = sprintf("w%02d", 1:n_item),
                log_freq = round(runif(n_item, 1, 6), 2),
                w0       = rnorm(n_item, 0, 30))                        # own difficulty

lexdec <- crossing(participants, words) |>
  mutate(freq_c = log_freq - mean(words$log_freq),
         rt = round(650 + u0 + w0 + (-30 + u1) * freq_c + rnorm(n(), 0, 50))) |>
  select(participant, word, log_freq, freq_c, rt)
```

. . .

The true frequency effect is −30 ms per log unit. But participants differ in speed and in the size of their frequency effect, and words differ in difficulty.

## 800 rows, but not 800 independent observations

```{r}
lexdec
count(lexdec, participant) |> head(3)
```

## Everyone together

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.4}
ggplot(lexdec, aes(x = freq_c, y = rt)) +
  geom_point(colour = pandan, alpha = 0.3, size = 1.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = hornbill, se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(x = "log frequency (centred)", y = "Reaction time (ms)")
```

One cloud of 800 points, one line. This is what `lm(rt ~ freq_c)` sees.

## One participant at a time

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.6}
ggplot(lexdec, aes(x = freq_c, y = rt)) +
  geom_point(colour = pandan, alpha = 0.35, size = 0.9) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = hornbill, se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ participant, nrow = 3) +
  labs(x = "log frequency (centred)", y = "RT (ms)") +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 11), axis.text = element_text(size = 9))
```

Every participant has their own level (fast or slow) and their own slope (a strong or weak frequency effect).

# The independence assumption

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` each naked mole-rat colony has its own [dialect]{.hl}. Researchers analysed over 30,000 soft chirps from seven colonies: the animals answered calls in their own colony's dialect and largely ignored the others.

_Sources: Barker et al. (2021), Science; Science News_
:::

## What goes wrong with `lm()`?

```{r}
tidy(lm(rt ~ freq_c, data = lexdec))
```

. . .

The estimate is fine. The standard error is computed as if we had 800 independent observations.

. . .

But we only have 20 participants. If we ran the experiment again with 20 new participants, the slope could easily change by more than this SE suggests.

## The residuals give it away

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.2}
augment(lm(rt ~ freq_c, data = lexdec)) |>
  mutate(participant = lexdec$participant) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(participant, .resid, FUN = median), y = .resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = mist, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_boxplot(fill = NA, colour = kingfisher, outlier.size = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Participant (ordered by median residual)", y = "Residual (ms)") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10, angle = 90, vjust = 0.5))
```

The residuals of one participant are mostly positive or mostly negative. Knowing who produced a data point tells us something about its residual: they are [not independent]{.hl}.

## Two sources of non-independence

Participants differ: some are faster than others, and some show bigger effects. Items differ too: some words are harder than others, for everyone.

. . .

Clark (1973) called ignoring item variation the __language-as-fixed-effect fallacy__: if our conclusions should hold for words in general, not just the 40 we tested, the words are a sample too.

## Discussion

Think of a study you would like to run, or one you have read.

- Which units does it measure more than once: speakers, words, texts, classes, recording sessions?
- Should the conclusions hold beyond the particular units in the study?

# Design and averaging

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` naked mole-rats can live for more than 30 years. In records of over 3,000 animals, their risk of dying [did not rise with age]{.hl}, unlike in any other mammal studied.

_Source: Ruby, Smith & Buffenstein (2018), eLife_
:::

## The traditional fix: averaging

Collapse the data so that each unit contributes one number. A __by-participant__ (F1) analysis: one frequency slope per participant, then test the 20 slopes.

```{r}
by_participant <- lexdec |>
  summarise(slope = coef(lm(rt ~ freq_c))[2], .by = participant)

t.test(by_participant$slope)$conf.int
```

## By-item analysis

A __by-item__ (F2) analysis: average over participants, one RT per word.

```{r}
by_word <- lexdec |> summarise(rt = mean(rt), freq_c = first(freq_c), .by = word)
tidy(lm(rt ~ freq_c, data = by_word))[2, ]
```

## Problems with averaging

- Two separate analyses, which can disagree: which one do we report?
- Averaging throws away information: variation within participants is lost
- With missing data or unbalanced designs, averages are based on different numbers of observations
- It is hard to include predictors that vary within a unit, such as trial number

. . .

Mixed models handle participants and items, in one model, on the raw data.

# Varying intercepts and slopes

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` the dialects are [learned]{.hl}: pups raised in another colony took on that colony's dialect. When a queen died, her colony's dialect became more variable, until a new queen took over.

_Sources: Barker et al. (2021), Science; Science News_
:::

## Fixed and random effects

A [linear mixed effects model]{.hl} extends linear regression to repeated measures. It mixes two kinds of terms:

| | Fixed effects | Random effects |
|:--|:--|:--|
| What they are | the effects of the predictors we are interested in | adjustments to those effects for each participant or word |
| Here | the frequency effect, `freq_c` | each participant's speed and frequency effect, each word's difficulty |
| Read like | the coefficients of `lm()` | how much the grouping units vary |

## Three ways to pool {.smaller}

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.4}
grid <- crossing(participant = unique(lexdec$participant),
                 freq_c = range(lexdec$freq_c))

m_complete <- lm(rt ~ freq_c, data = lexdec)
m_partial  <- lmer(rt ~ freq_c + (1 + freq_c | participant), data = lexdec)

lines <- bind_rows(
  grid |> mutate(fit = predict(m_complete, newdata = grid),
                 panel = "Complete pooling: one line"),
  lexdec |> group_by(participant) |>
    group_modify(\(d, k) tibble(freq_c = range(lexdec$freq_c),
                                fit = predict(lm(rt ~ freq_c, data = d),
                                              newdata = tibble(freq_c = range(lexdec$freq_c))))) |>
    ungroup() |> mutate(panel = "No pooling: 20 separate lines"),
  grid |> mutate(fit = predict(m_partial, newdata = grid),
                 panel = "Partial pooling: mixed model")
) |>
  mutate(panel = fct_inorder(panel))

ggplot(lines, aes(x = freq_c, y = fit, group = participant)) +
  geom_line(colour = kingfisher, alpha = 0.7, linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel) +
  labs(x = "log frequency (centred)", y = "Predicted RT (ms)")
```

Complete pooling ignores participants and is overconfident. No pooling treats each participant as unrelated to the others, which makes every line noisy. [Partial pooling]{.hl} treats participants as different but similar, drawn from one population.

## Varying intercepts

Each participant gets their own intercept: the overall intercept plus an adjustment.

<div class="formula">rt = (b₀ + u₀ⱼ) + b₁ · freq + e</div>

- `b₀`, `b₁`: the fixed effects, shared by everyone
- `u₀ⱼ`: participant j's adjustment, drawn from a normal distribution with mean 0 and an estimated SD

## Varying intercepts, visually

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4}
m_int <- lmer(rt ~ freq_c + (1 | participant), data = lexdec)
grid |>
  mutate(fit = predict(m_int, newdata = grid)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = freq_c, y = fit, group = participant)) +
  geom_line(colour = hornbill, alpha = 0.8, linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "log frequency (centred)", y = "RT (ms)")
```

Parallel lines: participants differ in speed but share the same frequency effect.

## Varying slopes

Each participant also gets their own slope:

<div class="formula">rt = (b₀ + u₀ⱼ) + (b₁ + u₁ⱼ) · freq + e</div>

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 2.9}
grid |>
  mutate(fit = predict(m_partial, newdata = grid)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = freq_c, y = fit, group = participant)) +
  geom_line(colour = hornbill, alpha = 0.8, linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "log frequency (centred)", y = "RT (ms)")
```

Now the lines fan out: some participants are much more sensitive to frequency than others.

## What the model estimates

The model does not estimate 20 separate intercepts and 20 separate slopes as free parameters. It estimates:

- the fixed effects: the average intercept and slope
- the SD of the intercepts across participants
- the SD of the slopes across participants
- the correlation between intercepts and slopes
- the residual SD

. . .

The participants' individual adjustments are then predicted from these, and from each participant's own data.

## Partial pooling = shrinkage

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.9}
shrink <- by_participant |>
  rename(no_pooling = slope) |>
  left_join(coef(m_partial)$participant |>
              rownames_to_column("participant") |>
              select(participant, partial_pooling = freq_c),
            by = "participant") |>
  mutate(participant = fct_reorder(participant, no_pooling))

ggplot(shrink, aes(y = participant)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = fixef(m_partial)["freq_c"], colour = mist, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = no_pooling, xend = partial_pooling, yend = participant),
               colour = moss, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.15, "cm"))) +
  geom_point(aes(x = no_pooling), colour = orchid, size = 2.5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = partial_pooling), colour = kingfisher, size = 2.5) +
  labs(x = "Frequency slope (ms per log unit)", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9))
```

Pink: each participant's own slope (no pooling). Blue: the mixed model's estimate. Extreme slopes are pulled, [shrunk]{.hl}, towards the average (dashed): the model borrows strength from the other participants.

# Interpreting random effects

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` naked mole-rat queens show no menopause. They stay [fertile past the age of 30]{.hl}.

_Source: Ruby, Smith & Buffenstein (2018), eLife_
:::

## Random effect SDs {.smaller}

```{r}
m_full <- lmer(rt ~ freq_c + (1 + freq_c | participant) + (1 | word), data = lexdec)
VarCorr(m_full)
```

. . .

| Row | Varies with an SD of about |
|:--|:--|
| `participant (Intercept)` | `r round(attr(VarCorr(m_full)$participant, "stddev")[1])` ms: participants' average RTs |
| `participant freq_c` | `r round(attr(VarCorr(m_full)$participant, "stddev")[2])` ms per log unit: their frequency slopes |
| `word (Intercept)` | `r round(attr(VarCorr(m_full)$word, "stddev")[1])` ms: how hard the words are |
| `Residual` | `r round(sigma(m_full))` ms: what is left, trial by trial |

## What an SD of 18 means

The average slope is `r round(fixef(m_full)["freq_c"], 1)` ms per log unit. With an SD of `r round(attr(VarCorr(m_full)$participant, "stddev")[2])` across participants, about 95% of participants should have slopes within ±2 SD:

```{r}
fixef(m_full)["freq_c"] + c(-2, 2) * attr(VarCorr(m_full)$participant, "stddev")["freq_c"]
```

. . .

A large random-effect SD means that participants differ a lot, even after accounting for frequency. A small one means they behave much alike.

## Random effect correlations

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.5}
coef(m_full)$participant |>
  ggplot(aes(x = `(Intercept)`, y = freq_c)) +
  geom_point(colour = kingfisher, size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = hornbill, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Participant intercept (ms, average RT)", y = "Participant frequency slope")
```

The model estimates a correlation of about `r round(attr(VarCorr(m_full)$participant, "correlation")[1, 2], 2)`: slower participants show stronger (more negative) frequency effects. Correlations like this can be theoretically interesting in their own right.

# The lme4 syntax

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` naked mole-rats can survive at least [18 minutes]{.hl} without any oxygen, by running their brain and heart on fructose instead of glucose.

_Sources: Park et al. (2017), Science; Max Delbrück Center_
:::

## Random effects in `lmer()` {.smaller}

The `{lme4}` package: `lmer()` works like `lm()`, plus random effects in brackets, `(effects | group)`.

| You write | Each group gets |
|:--|:--|
| `(1 \| participant)` | its own intercept |
| `(1 + freq_c \| participant)` | its own intercept and slope, and their correlation |
| `(1 + freq_c \|\| participant)` | its own intercept and slope, without a correlation |
| `(0 + freq_c \| participant)` | only its own slope |
| `(1 \| participant) + (1 \| word)` | [crossed]{.hl} effects: every participant sees every word |
| `(1 \| school / class)` | [nested]{.hl} effects: each class belongs to one school |

## Our model

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(lme4)
lmer(rt ~ freq_c + (1 + freq_c | participant) + (1 | word), data = lexdec)
```

The fixed effects, `rt ~ freq_c`, are written exactly as in `lm()`. Then each participant gets their own intercept and frequency slope, and each word its own intercept.

. . .

Why no `(1 + freq_c | word)`? Each word has one frequency. A slope needs variation in the predictor within the group: frequency varies within participants, but not within words.

## A first look at the output

```{r}
fixef(m_full)
```

. . .

The fixed effects read like `lm()` coefficients: an average RT of `r round(fixef(m_full)[1])` ms at average frequency, and `r round(fixef(m_full)[2], 1)` ms per log unit of frequency.

. . .

Next week: the full output, significance testing, likelihood ratio tests, and what to do when models do not converge.

# Why varying slopes matter

## Same estimate, different certainty {.smaller}

```{r}
models <- list(
  "lm(rt ~ freq_c)"                                = lm(rt ~ freq_c, data = lexdec),
  "+ (1 | participant)"                            = lmer(rt ~ freq_c + (1 | participant), data = lexdec),
  "+ (1 + freq_c | participant)"                   = lmer(rt ~ freq_c + (1 + freq_c | participant), data = lexdec),
  "+ (1 + freq_c | participant) + (1 | word)"      = m_full
)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
tibble(model = names(models),
       estimate = map_dbl(models, \(m) coef(summary(m))["freq_c", "Estimate"]),
       SE       = map_dbl(models, \(m) coef(summary(m))["freq_c", "Std. Error"])) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

. . .

The estimate is the same in every model. The standard error is not: random intercepts alone make it smaller than `lm()`, and varying slopes make it about three times larger than with random intercepts alone.

## Why?

With random intercepts only, the model assumes every participant has the same frequency effect. All 800 trials then count as evidence about one slope.

. . .

But participants differ in their slopes. To generalise to new participants, the model must know how much slopes vary, and that uncertainty belongs in the SE.

. . .

Barr et al. (2013) showed that random-intercept-only models can have Type I error rates well above 5%, and recommend the __maximal random effects structure justified by the design__ for confirmatory tests.

## Compare with averaging

```{r, echo = FALSE}
tibble(
  analysis = c("By-participant (F1) analysis",
               "Mixed model, (1 + freq_c | participant)"),
  SE = c(sd(by_participant$slope) / sqrt(nrow(by_participant)),
         coef(summary(models[[3]]))["freq_c", "Std. Error"])
) |>
  mutate(SE = round(SE, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

. . .

With varying slopes, the mixed model is about as cautious as the by-participant analysis, while keeping all the data, and adding words in the same model.

# Different interpretations

## What is a random effect?

There is no single answer. Gelman (2005) lists five definitions in use, summarised by Coretta (2021):

1. __Constant vs varying__: fixed coefficients are constant across individuals; random coefficients vary (Kreft & de Leeuw, 1998)
2. __Researcher's interest__: effects are fixed if the research question is about them; random if the interest lies in the underlying population (Searle, Casella & McCulloch)
3. __Sampling__: "When a sample exhausts the population, the corresponding variable is fixed"; when the sample is a negligible part of it, the variable is random (Green & Tukey, 1960)

## What is a random effect?

4. __Random variable__: "If an effect is assumed to be a realized value of a random variable, it is called a random effect" (LaMotte, 1983)
5. __Estimation__: fixed effects are estimated by least squares or maximum likelihood; random effects are estimated with [shrinkage]{.hl}, that is, partial pooling (Snijders & Bosker)

. . .

The definitions often disagree. Is "word" random because the words are a sample (3), because they vary (1), or because their estimates are shrunk (5)?

## So which is it?

- Gelman recommends avoiding "fixed" and "random" altogether: effects are [constant]{.hl} or [varying]{.hl} across groups
- In Bayesian work, [population-level]{.hl} and [group-level]{.hl} effects are increasingly common terms
- In practice: a grouping factor gets random effects when its levels are a sample from a larger population (participants, words, speakers), and you want to generalise beyond them

. . .

Whatever the label, ask: which units are repeated in my data, and which effects can vary across them?

# Your turn

## Which random effects?

For each design, name the grouping factors, and the varying slopes the design allows:

1. 30 speakers each read 50 sentences, half of them questions and half statements. Outcome: final pitch rise.
2. 24 children are recorded at ages 2, 3 and 4. Outcome: vocabulary size.
3. 40 participants rate 60 words for emotional valence. Each word has one frequency and one length.

## Possible answers

1. Speakers and sentences. `(1 + type | speaker) + (1 | sentence)`: type varies within speakers, but each sentence is one type
2. Children. `(1 + age | child)`: age varies within each child
3. Participants and words. `(1 + frequency + length | participant) + (1 | word)`: frequency and length vary within participants, not within words

## Summary

::: {.takeaway}
- Repeated measures violate [independence]{.hl}: data points from the same unit are alike
- Ignoring this makes SEs too small; averaging throws information away
- Mixed models add [varying intercepts]{.hl} and [varying slopes]{.hl} for each grouping factor
- They estimate the SD of these adjustments, and [shrink]{.hl} individual estimates towards the average
- `(1 + x | participant) + (1 | item)`: slopes only for predictors that vary within the group
- "Random effect" has several meanings: think [constant]{.hl} vs [varying]{.hl}
:::
